summary: Updates RFC 5247 to define how an EAP Session-Id is derived for several authentication methods. It fills a gap for EAP-SIM and EAP-AKA when a fast reconnect is used instead of full authentication, and also clarifies the derivation for other methods including PEAP.

eli5.summary: When you rejoin a network quickly after a short break, both sides need the same name for your session. This explains how to work out that name for a few login methods.

subtitle: Fills the gaps in how EAP-SIM, EAP-AKA and PEAP name a session, including after a fast reconnect.

tldr.problem: RFC 5247 defined the EAP Session-Id for EAP-SIM and EAP-AKA only for full authentication, in ambiguous text, and never defined it for PEAP. Fast reconnect had no Session-Id at all.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC replaces the Appendix A text of RFC 5247 with clear formulas: full authentication and fast reconnect each get their own for EAP-SIM and EAP-AKA, and PEAP gets one that is the same for both cases.
tldr.outcome: Systems such as ERP, which need the Session-Id, can now work with fast reconnect for EAP-SIM and EAP-AKA, and with PEAP. The RFC updates RFC 5247.

today: RFC 8940 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5247, and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself says its definitions are widely deployed in major EAP implementations.

sections.title: Why a Session-Id Fix Was Needed
sections.content:
An EAP Session-Id is a value that names an authentication session. RFC 5247 defined it for EAP-SIM and EAP-AKA, but only for full authentication. EAP-SIM and EAP-AKA also have an optional fast reconnect exchange, and there the old formula could not be used.

The text in RFC 5247 was also ambiguous even for full authentication, and it never defined a Session-Id for PEAP. RFC 8940 fixes all three problems.

The IEEE Fast Initial Link Setup (FILS) authentication needs the EAP Session-Id so that the EAP Re-authentication Protocol (ERP, RFC 6696) can work. That is why the gaps mattered. EAP-AKA' is left out because another document defines it.
sections.eli5: Both sides of a login need to agree on a name for it. The old rules only worked for the first, slow login, not for the quick re-login, so this fills the hole.

sections.title: EAP-AKA Session-Id
sections.content:
For full authentication, the EAP-AKA Session-Id is the EAP Type Code 0x17, followed by the RAND field from the AT_RAND attribute, followed by the AUTN field from the AT_AUTN attribute. The RFC writes this as 0x17 || RAND || AUTN.

For fast reconnect, those fields are not used. Instead the Session-Id is 0x17, then the NONCE_S field from AT_NONCE_S, then the MAC field from AT_MAC in the EAP-Request/AKA-Reauthentication message: 0x17 || NONCE_S || MAC.
sections.eli5: The name of the login is built by gluing together a few random-looking values from the messages. The quick re-login uses different values than the first login.

sections.title: EAP-SIM Session-Id
sections.content:
For full authentication, the EAP-SIM Session-Id starts with the EAP Type Code 0x12, then the RAND values, then the NONCE_MT field from AT_NONCE_MT. RFC 4186 says the server obtains "n" GSM triplets, where n is 2 or 3, and each triplet contributes one RAND.

  • For n=2: 0x12 || RAND1 || RAND2 || NONCE_MT, which is 49 octets long.
  • For n=3: 0x12 || RAND1 || RAND2 || RAND3 || NONCE_MT, which is 65 octets long.

For fast reconnect, the Session-Id is 0x12 || NONCE_S || MAC, using the MAC from the EAP-Request/SIM/Reauthentication message. It is 33 octets long.
sections.eli5: EAP-SIM works the same way as EAP-AKA, but it can glue in two or three random values from the SIM, so the name comes out longer.

sections.title: Rationale for the Changes
sections.content:
Appendix A of RFC 5247 was meant to define exported parameters for existing EAP methods. The old EAP-SIM and EAP-AKA definitions used RAND, AUTN and NONCE_MT, which are not used in fast reconnect.

Based on RFC 4187 and RFC 4186, NONCE_S plays the role of RAND, and the MAC in the reauthentication request plays the role of AUTN (or NONCE_MT for EAP-SIM). So NONCE_S and MAC can stand in for them.

The value comes from a random value made by the server, a secret key and the peer's identity. The author believes it is secure, though no formal analysis has been done.
sections.eli5: On a quick re-login, the usual ingredients are missing, so the document swaps in the ingredients that play the same role.

sections.title: Session-Id for PEAP
sections.content:
RFC 5247 did not define a Session-Id for Microsoft's Protected EAP (PEAP). For consistency with EAP-TLS (RFC 5216), the RFC defines it as 0x19 || client.random || server.random.

The definition is the same for full authentication and for fast reconnect. The RFC says it is already in widespread use in all known PEAP implementations.

It applies only when TLS 1.2 or earlier is used. A different derivation for TLS 1.3 is defined in a separate document.
sections.eli5: PEAP gets its own name recipe too: a code number plus the random values each side picked at the start. It is the same recipe for first and quick logins.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
These definitions let ERP key hierarchies be set up after a fast reconnect with EAP-SIM and EAP-AKA. The RFC states that the Session-Ids are unique per session, unforgeable and unguessable by an outside party, as RFC 5247 requires.

The definitions have been widely deployed for years in all major EAP implementations, but the RFC admits that very little security analysis has been done, and that any security issues would be serious. The security considerations of RFC 5247 are not changed. There are no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: The names are meant to be unique and hard to guess. People have used them for years, but nobody has checked them very carefully on paper.
